plan.title: How Costco Gets You to Spend More (and Still Feel Like You Saved)
plan.description:
Why do you go to Costco for milk and leave with a kayak? We break down the treasure-hunt store design, the markup caps, and the membership machine that earns Costco billions, using its fiscal 2025 annual report. Plus: is it actually saving you money?

Chapters:
0:00 The $300 receipt
0:44 The treasure hunt
1:50 The price ceiling
2:56 The real business
4:02 Is it actually saving you money?
4:47 How to beat the machine

Sources:
https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/909832/000090983225000101/cost-20250831.htm
https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/costco-reports-higher-sales-and-earnings-q4-and-fiscal-year
https://fortune.com/article/costco-promises-hot-dog-drink-combo-will-always-be-1-50
https://finance.yahoo.com/news/costco-reveals-keeps-prices-low-183300293.html
https://chowhound.com/1540007/costco-shopping-grocery-treasure-hunts

The opening shopping trip is an illustrative example. Narration is AI-generated. Educational content only, not financial advice.

segments.narration: You walk into Costco for milk and a rotisserie chicken.
Forty minutes later, you're at the checkout with a kayak, a tub of cashews and a three hundred dollar receipt.
And somehow, you walk out feeling like you just saved money.
That feeling is not an accident. It's the whole business.
Last year Costco sold almost two hundred and seventy billion dollars of stuff.
But it makes surprisingly little profit on any of it.
So where does the money really come from? And is Costco actually saving you money, or is it getting you?
By the end of this video, you'll know exactly how the machine works. And how to beat it.
It starts the second you walk through the door.
The things you actually came for, like toilet paper and cleaning supplies, sit in separate corners of the store.
Costco calls them trigger items. And it moves them around, so you have to cross the whole warehouse to find them.
Which means you walk straight past the middle of the store.
That's where the treasure is. Marked down steaks, wine, vacuum cleaners, even diamond rings.
And here's the catch. Costco rotates its products faster than most stores.
So every member learns the same rule. If you see it, buy it. Next week it might be gone.
That's not a shopping trip. It's a treasure hunt. And the urgency is built into the floor plan.
There's another trick hiding in plain sight. There just isn't much to choose from.
A typical Costco warehouse carries fewer than four thousand active products.
A regular supermarket can carry tens of thousands.
Less choice means faster decisions. And faster decisions mean fuller carts.
Now, the deals themselves are real. And this is the part most people miss.
According to retail industry reports, Costco caps its markup at about fourteen percent on outside brands.
And about fifteen percent on its own Kirkland Signature products.
Put that together and Costco's gross margin in 2025 was only about eleven percent.
In plain words, sell a hundred dollars of goods, and only around eleven dollars is left after paying for the goods.
And that eleven dollars still has to pay the staff, the rent and the trucks.
Costco's finance chief says the goal is to be first to cut prices for members, and last to raise them.
The most famous proof? The hot dog and soda combo. It has cost a dollar fifty since 1985.
When an executive once warned founder Jim Sinegal it was losing money, his reported reply was, raise it and I'll kill you. Figure it out.
So if Costco barely profits on the stuff in your cart, how does it earn billions?
The answer is in your wallet.
A basic Costco membership in the United States costs sixty five dollars a year.
At the end of fiscal 2025, there were about eighty one million paid memberships.
Together those fees brought in about five point three billion dollars.
Now compare that to Costco's total profit for the year. About eight point one billion dollars.
The fees alone are worth roughly two thirds of the company's entire profit.
And a fee costs almost nothing to collect. No pallets. No trucks. No shelf space.
Then there's the upgrade. The Executive tier costs another sixty five dollars and pays a cash reward on what you spend.
About thirty eight point seven million members took it. Close to half of everyone.
And here's the real test of the machine.
In September 2024, Costco raised its fees in the United States and Canada.
Renewal rates barely moved. About ninety two percent of members there still renewed in 2025.
Most gyms and streaming services would kill for that.
So, back to that three hundred dollar receipt.
segments.chapter: Is it actually saving you money?

segments.narration: On the things you planned to buy, Costco is hard to beat. The markup caps make sure of that.
But the treasure hunt is designed to sell you things you didn't plan to buy.
And a bulk pack only saves money if you actually finish it. A crate of avocados that goes brown is not a deal.
Here's the clever part. Costco wins either way.
If you save, you feel smart, and you renew. If you overspend, Costco still earns its slim margin on every item.
Your cart is not where Costco makes its money. Your cart is the proof the membership is worth it.
So how do you beat it? Shop it the way Costco's own buyers would.
Bring a list. Treat the middle of the store like a museum. Look, don't touch.
Only buy bulk on things you already use every single week.
And do the maths on the Executive tier. It only pays if your reward is bigger than the extra sixty five dollars.
Costco isn't really selling you groceries. It's selling you the feeling of a great deal.
And it might be the best company on the planet at doing it.
If you want more breakdowns like this, subscribe. We follow the money behind a famous company every week.

plan.originality_note: Viewer-centric angle: follows one shopping trip through the store psychology, the markup caps and the membership maths, then answers whether it really saves you money and how to shop it smarter.
